1-1-1: Good intentions, ready for a clear nutrition plan

Your team cares about what students eat, and menus already balance taste, variety and cost. Nutrition is not yet planned, measured or protected by set limits, so it depends on daily choices rather than a system.
Start with one step: set age-wise nutrition targets with a nutritionist before the next menu cycle, then add simple limits on fried and sugary items.
You become the leader who put a clear nutrition plan in place, with something concrete to share at the next parent or board meeting.
A visible food plan answers one of the first questions families ask when choosing an institution, and it protects your name whenever food is discussed.
Parents get a straight answer about what their child eats, and students keep the favourites they enjoy, made better.
1-1-3: Limits on some items are a good start; the plan behind them comes next

You already limit some less healthy items, such as fried snacks or sugary drinks, which shows real intent. Menus are still led by taste and budget, and there is little data to show how nutritious the meals are.
Turn the limits you have into a plan: set age-wise nutrition targets, then extend clear standards across the full menu.
You can show that today's limits were the first step of a deliberate plan, not a one-off rule.
Consistent standards stop the food from becoming a talking point for the wrong reasons among parents.
Families see healthier choices become the norm rather than the exception.
1-1-5: Strong ingredient rules, waiting for a plan and proof

Clear limits on sugar, salt, fried and processed food, with fresh ingredients as the default, put you ahead of many institutions. What is missing is a plan that starts from nutrition targets, and data that proves the result.
Build on your standards: set age-wise targets for each menu, then measure nutrient values for your most-served dishes.
Your ingredient standards become a story you can prove with numbers, not just describe.
Evidence behind your standards turns good practice into a reputation families trust and recommend to others.
Parents can see the care behind every plate, and students enjoy fresh food made the right way.
1-3-1: Some nutrition data in hand; the plan and limits come next
You can already share nutrition information for some meals, which many institutions cannot. Menus are still shaped mostly by taste and budget, and there are no set limits on less healthy items.
Use the data you have to set age-wise nutrition targets, and agree simple limits on fried, sugary and salty foods.
You turn occasional data into a plan you can present with confidence.
A clear plan gives families a reason to trust your food, and heads off complaints before they start.
Parents get consistent answers for the whole menu, not just a few meals.
1-3-3: Data and some limits in place; menus now need a nutrition-first plan

Partial nutrition data and limits on some items show a cafeteria moving in the right direction. Because menus still start from taste and budget, the good practice is not yet consistent across every meal.
Make nutrition the starting point: set age-wise targets before each menu cycle, then extend data and limits to the full menu.
You lead the shift from good habits to a nutrition programme with your name on it.
Consistency is what families notice and talk about, and it is what sets one institution apart from another.
Students get balanced meals every day, not only on good days.
1-3-5: Strong standards and growing data, ready for nutrition-first menus
Clear ingredient standards and nutrition data for some meals give you a solid base. The next gain is planning: menus still begin with taste and budget rather than nutrition targets.
Set age-wise nutrition targets with a nutritionist and design the next menu cycle around them; then extend your data to every menu.
You complete the picture of standards, data and a plan, a story worth sharing with your board.
A complete, nutrition-led programme is a clear point of difference when families compare institutions.
Parents see that every meal is planned for their child's age, not just kept within limits.
1-5-1: You can prove the numbers; now shape the menu around them

Measuring every menu against benchmarks with a nutritionist's review is rare and valuable. The data is likely to show gaps, because menus are planned around taste and budget and there are no set limits on less healthy items.
Use your data to act: set age-wise targets, and introduce clear limits on sugar, salt, fried and processed foods.
You already have the evidence; acting on it makes you the leader who turned measurement into results.
Data that leads to visible change builds the kind of trust that keeps families with you year after year.
Families see the numbers improve term by term.
1-5-3: Strong measurement and some limits; planning is the missing piece
Full nutrition data and limits on some items show you take nutrition seriously. Menus are still led by taste and budget, so the data is measuring a menu that was not designed for nutrition.
Let your data lead: set age-wise targets first, design menus to meet them, and extend your limits to the full menu.
You can show a closed loop, from targets to menus to measured results.
A programme that plans, measures and improves is easy to explain to families and inspectors alike.
Students get food designed for their needs, and parents can see the proof.
1-5-5: Proof and standards in place; one step from nutrition by design
Clear ingredient standards and measured nutrition data for every menu put you well ahead. The one gap is planning: menus start from taste and budget instead of age-wise nutrition targets.
Make targets the first step of every menu cycle, so your chefs design to them and your data confirms them.
This single change completes a programme you can present as best practice.
Nutrition by design, backed by data, gives families a strong reason to choose you and stay.
Parents get meals planned for their child's age, with numbers to show the plan works.
3-1-1: Balanced menus in place; proof and limits come next
Menus built around food groups and seasonal produce show real care. There is little data to prove nutrition yet, and no set limits on sugar, salt, fried or processed food.
Add simple limits on less healthy items, then measure nutrient values for your most-served dishes.
You move from "we try to serve balanced meals" to "here is how we know", a much stronger position for any leader.
Evidence and clear rules protect your reputation and make your food programme easy to recommend.
Parents get answers backed by facts, and students get balanced meals with fewer fried and sugary extras.
3-1-3: Balance and some limits in place; proof is the next step
Balanced menus and limits on some items give you a good foundation. What is missing is data: there is little to show parents or leaders how nutritious the food really is.
Measure nutrient values for your top dishes, show them on the menu board, and extend your limits to the full menu.
You gain evidence to back the care your team already puts in.
Being able to show the facts turns a good cafeteria into a selling point for the whole institution.
Parents can see what is on the plate, not just be told about it.
3-1-5: Balanced menus and clear standards; now show the proof
Balanced menus and clear limits on less healthy food mean your students are eating well. Today you can only share menus and ingredient lists, so this good work is hard to prove.
Measure nutrient values for every menu against benchmarks, reviewed by a nutritionist, and share a simple summary with families.
Proof turns your strongest work into recognition you can point to.
Families talk about what they can see; visible nutrition data turns good food into reputation.
Parents get evidence of the care that already goes into their child's meals.
3-3-1: Balanced menus and some data; healthy limits come next
Balanced menus and nutrition data for some meals show steady progress. Without set limits, fried, sugary and processed items can still undo good planning.
Agree clear limits, for example fried snacks no more than twice a week and water as the default drink, and make healthier versions of favourites.
Clear standards are a simple, visible decision that families notice and remember.
Fewer fried and sugary items remove one of the most common sources of parent concern.
Students still get the favourites they love, made healthier, and parents worry less.
3-3-3: Good practice in every area, ready to become consistent
You have balanced menus, some nutrition data and limits on some items. Each is a good start; none is yet consistent across the full menu.
Complete one area first, ideally age-wise nutrition targets, then extend data and limits step by step.
You lead the move from good practice to a complete, consistent programme.
Consistency is what turns a good cafeteria into one that families recommend.
Students get the same quality every day, and parents get clear answers every time.
3-3-5: Clear standards and balanced menus; targets and full data next
Clear ingredient standards, balanced menus and some nutrition data give you a strong base. The next gains are planning to age-wise targets and measuring every menu.
Set age-wise targets for the next menu cycle and extend nutrient analysis to every menu, reviewed by a nutritionist.
Two focused steps take you to a programme you can present as best practice.
A measurable, nutrition-led cafeteria is a clear advantage when families compare institutions.
Parents see the full picture, and students eat meals planned for their age.
3-5-1: Strong proof and balanced menus; healthy limits will lift the results
Full nutrition data and balanced menus show a mature approach. Without set limits, though, fried, sugary and processed items still have a place on the menu, and your data will show it.
Use your data to set clear limits on sugar, salt, fried and processed foods, and track the change term by term.
You can show measurable improvement, the strongest kind of recognition.
Visible, measured change gives families a concrete reason to trust your food.
Parents see healthier menus, with the numbers to prove it.
3-5-3: Strong data and balanced menus; extend limits and set targets
Measured nutrition data and balanced menus put you ahead of most institutions. Limits cover only some items, and menus are balanced rather than built to age-wise targets.
Extend your limits to the full menu, then set age-wise targets so your data measures against clear goals.
Your data already proves effort; targets let it prove results.
Clear goals and measured progress make your food programme easy to present to families and your board.
Students get consistently healthier food, and parents can see it clearly.
3-5-5: Strong proof and standards; age-wise targets complete the picture
Measured nutrition data and clear ingredient standards make this a strong area. Menus are balanced, but not yet designed from age-wise nutrition targets.
Set age-wise targets with a nutritionist and design each menu cycle to meet them.
You complete a nutrition programme you can present as a model for others.
A programme this complete is a lasting point of difference for the institution.
Every age group gets food planned for its needs, with proof to share.
5-1-1: Nutrition targets lead; now prove and protect them
Starting menus from age-wise nutrition targets is the hardest part, and you have done it. There is little data yet to show the targets are met, and no set limits on less healthy items.
Measure nutrient values for your top dishes against your targets, and add clear limits on sugar, salt, fried and processed foods.
Proof turns a strong plan into results you can show.
A plan with evidence behind it is a powerful message for families and inspectors.
Parents see that the plan reaches their child's plate.
5-1-3: A strong plan and some limits; proof is the next step
Nutrition targets lead your menus and some limits are in place, a solid foundation. What is missing is the data to show parents and leaders that the plan works.
Measure every menu against your targets with a nutritionist's review, and extend your limits to the full menu.
You gain the evidence to show your plan delivers.
Data behind your plan turns good practice into reputation.
Parents get clear, factual answers about their child's meals.
5-1-5: A strong plan and strong standards; now show the proof
Nutrition-first menus and clear ingredient standards mean students are eating well. Today you can share menus and ingredient lists, but not measured nutrition data.
Add nutrient analysis for every menu, checked against benchmarks, and share a simple summary with families.
This is the step that turns your strongest work into recognition.
When families can see the proof, good food becomes a reason to choose you.
Parents get evidence of what they hoped was true.
5-3-1: A strong plan and growing data; set limits to protect it
Nutrition targets lead your menus and you have data for some meals. Without set limits, fried, sugary and processed items can still work against the plan.
Agree clear limits with fresh, whole ingredients as the default, and extend your data to every menu.
Clear standards make your plan visible to every student and parent.
Fewer less healthy items remove the most common source of parent concern.
Students keep their favourites, made healthier, and parents worry less.
5-3-3: Nutrition by design, with data and limits still growing
Menus built from age-wise targets show real commitment. Data covers some meals and limits cover some items, so the plan is not yet fully proven or protected.
Extend nutrient analysis to every menu and limits to the full menu, with a nutritionist's review each term.
Two extensions turn a strong plan into a complete programme.
A complete, proven programme is easy for families to trust and recommend.
Parents see the full picture, every day.
5-3-5: A strong plan and standards; full data is the final step
Nutrition-first menus and clear ingredient standards make this a strong area. Data covers some meals, so part of your good work is still unproven.
Extend nutrient analysis to every menu and share it on the menu board or through a parent app.
Full data lets you present this area as a model.
Visible proof turns strong practice into a lasting reputation.
Parents can check any meal, on any day.
5-5-1: Planned and proven; healthy limits are the gap
Age-wise targets and measured data for every menu are a rare combination. The gap is on the plate: there are no set limits on sugar, salt, fried and processed food.
Set clear limits, make fresh, whole ingredients the default, and use your data to track the change.
Closing this one gap gives you a complete programme to present.
This removes the most visible point of concern for families.
Students get favourites made healthier, and parents see the improvement in the numbers.
5-5-3: Planned and proven; extend your limits to the full menu
Nutrition targets lead your menus and every menu is measured against benchmarks. Limits cover only some items, so less healthy food still appears in places.
Extend your ingredient standards across the full menu and track the effect in your data.
You can show a programme that plans, proves and improves.
This level of rigour is a lasting point of difference.
Parents get consistency and proof across every meal.
5-5-5: Nutrition by design, proven and protected
Menus start from age-wise targets, every menu is measured against benchmarks, and clear standards keep less healthy food in check. This is what a future-ready cafeteria looks like.
Keep it fresh: share results with families each term, and use your data to introduce new dishes students love.
You lead a programme that others can learn from, and that is worth presenting widely.
A proven nutrition programme is a lasting reason for families to choose you and stay.
Parents have full confidence in every meal, and students enjoy food that is good for them.
